340.title: Matter usually exists in one of three everyday states

members.title: Matter usually exists in one of three everyday states
members.content: Matter usually exists in one of three everyday states: solid, liquid, and gas. What state matter is in depends on two things: how closely packed its particles are, and how much energy (movement) those particles have.

members.title: What Is Matter? (Part 1 of 2)
members.content:
Matter is anything that has mass and takes up space.
Your desk, the air you breathe, the water you drink, and even you are all made of matter.
Scientists sort matter into three common states based on how its particles are arranged and how they move: solid, liquid, and gas.

members.title: What Is Matter? (Part 2 of 2)
members.content: Each state has its own shape, volume, and particle behavior, but all matter is made of the same kinds of tiny particles — what changes between the states is how closely packed those particles are and how much energy they have.

340.title: Particle arrangement in solids, liquids, and gases

members.title: Particle arrangement in solids, liquids, and gases
members.content: The image shows three arrangements of particles representing solids, liquids, and gases. In the first, the solid shows particles tightly packed together in fixed positions, suggesting a rigid structure. The second arrangement depicts particles close together but able to move, indicating a fluid state. Finally, the third shows particles far apart and moving freely, representing a gaseous state where movement is unrestricted.

members.title: As a general rule
members.content: As a general rule: the more energy particles have, the faster they move and the further apart they spread. Solids have the least particle energy and movement; gases have the most.

members.title: Matter
members.content: Matter is anything that has mass and occupies space. A book, water, air, a spoon, and a balloon all contain matter. Matter can be described using observable properties such as shape, volume, texture, color, and how it behaves inside a container.

members.title: Solid
members.content: A solid has a definite shape and a definite volume. Its particles are packed closely together and mainly vibrate in fixed positions. Examples include a stone, pencil, wooden block, and ice cube.

members.title: Solids
members.content: In a solid, particles are packed tightly together in a fixed, orderly pattern. They vibrate in place but do not move past one another.

members.title: Diagram description (Solids)
members.content: particles in a solid are drawn as evenly spaced dots arranged in tidy rows and columns, like a grid, showing a fixed, orderly pattern.

members.title: Key properties of solids
members.content:
Has a fixed shape -- it does not change shape unless a force is applied.
Has a fixed volume -- it takes up the same amount of space no matter what container it is in.
Particles are tightly packed and only vibrate in place.
Generally difficult to compress (squeeze into a smaller space).
Everyday examples:
ice cubes, a wooden chair, a rock, a coin, and a book.

members.title: Solids (Part 1 of 2)
members.content:
In a solid, particles are packed tightly together in a fixed pattern.
They vibrate in place but do not move past one another.
Because of this, a solid keeps a definite shape and a definite volume — it does not change shape to fit a container.

members.title: Solids (Part 2 of 2)
members.content:
Everyday examples:
An ice cube keeps its shape whether it sits in a bowl or on a plate.
A wooden block stays the same size and shape no matter where you put it.
A rock does not flow or spread out like a liquid would.
Key idea: solid particles are held in place by strong forces between them, so heating a solid makes the particles vibrate faster until, at the melting point, they break free of their fixed positions and the solid becomes a liquid.

members.title: Liquid
members.content:
A liquid has a definite volume but no definite shape. It flows and takes the shape of its container. Its particles are close together but can slide past one another.
Examples include water, milk, and cooking oil.

members.title: Liquids
members.content: In a liquid, particles are still close together, but they have more energy than in a solid. They can slide past one another, which is why liquids can flow and change shape.

members.title: Diagram description (Liquids)
members.content: particles in a liquid are drawn as dots that are close together but scattered in an irregular, flowing arrangement rather than a neat grid, showing that they can move around each other.

members.title: Key properties of liquids
members.content:
Has no fixed shape -- it takes the shape of its container.
Has a fixed volume -- the amount of liquid stays the same even if the container changes.
Particles can slide past each other, allowing the liquid to flow.
Generally difficult to compress, though slightly easier than a solid.
Everyday examples:
water, milk, cooking oil, and juice.

members.title: Liquids (Part 1 of 2)
members.content:
In a liquid, particles are still close together, but they are free to slide past one another.
This gives a liquid a definite volume but no fixed shape — it takes the shape of whatever container holds it, while the amount of liquid stays the same.

members.title: Liquids (Part 2 of 2)
members.content:
Everyday examples:
Water poured from a bottle into a cup changes shape but not amount.
Juice flows and settles at the bottom of any container you pour it into.
Cooking oil spreads out flat when poured onto a pan.
Key idea: heating a liquid gives its particles enough energy to escape into the air entirely, a process called evaporation, which turns the liquid into a gas at its boiling point.

members.title: Gas
members.content: A gas has no definite shape and no definite volume. It spreads out and fills the available space in its container. Its particles are far apart and move freely. Air and water vapor are examples of gases.

members.title: Gases
members.content: In a gas, particles have the most energy of the three states. They move quickly in every direction and spread far apart, filling all the space available to them.

members.title: Diagram description (Gases)
members.content: particles in a gas are drawn as widely spaced dots, each with a short line beside it representing fast, free movement in many directions.

members.title: Key properties of gases
members.content:
Has no fixed shape and no fixed volume -- it spreads out to fill its container completely.
Particles move quickly and freely, with large spaces between them.
Easy to compress because there is so much empty space between particles.
Everyday examples:
the air around you, helium in a balloon, and steam rising from a hot drink.

members.title: Gases (Part 1 of 2)
members.content:
In a gas, particles are spread far apart and move quickly in every direction.
A gas has no definite shape and no definite volume — it expands to completely fill whatever container it is in.

members.title: Gases (Part 2 of 2)
members.content:
Everyday examples:
The air inside a balloon spreads out evenly to fill the whole balloon.
Steam rising from a hot cup of tea spreads out into the room.
A helium tank fills every party balloon you attach to it, one at a time.
Key idea: cooling a gas slows its particles down until they pack close enough together to form a liquid again, a process called condensation.

members.title: Comparing the Three States
members.content: The table below summarizes the key differences. Row and column headers are labeled with text so the comparison does not depend on color alone.

members.title: 5. Comparing the Three States
members.content: The table shows three columns, labeled ‘Property’, ‘Solid’, ‘Liquid’, and ‘Gas’. The first row lists the properties being compared: shape, volume, particle spacing, particle movement, and compressibility. The ‘Solid’ column indicates that solids have a fixed shape and a fixed volume, with their particles vibrating closely together. In contrast, the ‘Liquid’ column shows that liquids take the shape of their container, have a fixed volume, and their particles slide past each other with a closer spacing than solids. Finally, the ‘Gas’ column describes that gases take the shape of their container, fill available space, have a far apart particle spacing, move quickly and freely, and are highly compressible.

members.title: Shape
members.content: Solids keep their shape; liquids and gases take the shape of their container.

members.title: Volume
members.content: Solids and liquids have definite volume; gases expand to fill available space.

members.title: Particle arrangement
members.content: Solid particles are tightly packed, liquid particles are close but mobile, and gas particles are widely spaced.

members.title: Flow
members.content: Liquids and gases can flow, while solids normally do not.

members.title: Comparing the Three States
members.content: The figure shows three columns comparing the properties of solids, liquids, and gases. In the first column, solids are shown to have a fixed shape and a fixed volume, with their particles packed very closely together and vibrating in place. The second column describes liquids as having a shape that takes the shape of the container they are in, maintaining a fixed volume, with their particles close together and sliding past each other. Finally, the third column indicates that gases fill the entire container, have no fixed volume, and their particles are far apart, moving freely and fast.

340.title: Changing From One State to Another

members.title: Changing From One State to Another
members.content: Adding or removing heat energy can change matter from one state to another. These changes are called changes of state. The names below describe the direction of each change.

members.title: How Matter Changes State
members.content:
Matter can change from one state to another when heat energy is added or removed. Adding heat makes particles move faster and spread apart (melting, then evaporation). Removing heat makes particles slow down and move closer together (condensation, then freezing). These changes are physical changes: the substance is still the same material, just arranged differently.
Melting — solid to liquid, caused by adding heat.
Freezing — liquid to solid, caused by removing heat.
Evaporation — liquid to gas, caused by adding heat.
Condensation — gas to liquid, caused by removing heat.

340.title: 6. Changing From One State to Another

members.title: 6. Changing From One State to Another
members.content: The figure shows a table outlining changes between states of matter. It lists four changes: melting, freezing, evaporating, and condensing. The first entry describes melting, showing a change from a solid to a liquid, and indicates that energy is added, causing the particles to move faster and spread out. The second entry details freezing, where a liquid transforms into a solid, and energy is removed, resulting in the particles slowing down and locking into place. The third entry explains evaporating or boiling, where a liquid becomes a gas, and energy is added, allowing the particles to move fast enough to escape and spread far apart. Finally, the fourth entry describes condensing, where a gas turns back into a liquid, and energy is removed, causing the particles to slow down and move closer together.

members.title: Example (Part 1 of 2)
members.content:
Example: an ice cube (solid) left on a counter absorbs heat from the air.
It melts into water (liquid).
If that water is heated on a stove until it boils, some of it evaporates into water vapor (gas).

members.title: Example (Part 2 of 2)
members.content:
Everyday Examples:
Water is one of the few substances people commonly see in all three states.
The table below lists a few examples for each state.
Try it yourself: look around the room you are in right now and name one solid, one liquid, and one gas you can find nearby.

members.title: 7. Everyday Examples
members.content: The table is arranged into three columns, labelled ‘Solid’, ‘Liquid’, and ‘Gas’. The first column lists ice, wood, rock, and a metal spoon, while the second column lists water, cooking oil, milk, and juice. The third column lists water vapor or steam, helium, air, and carbon dioxide in soda. Each item in the first two columns is paired with a corresponding item in the third column, indicating examples of each state of matter.

members.title: Summary: what to remember (Part 1 of 2)
members.content:
Matter is made of particles and commonly exists as a solid, liquid, or gas.
Solids hold a fixed shape and volume because their particles are tightly packed.
Liquids keep a fixed volume but flow to fit their container because their particles can slide past each other.

members.title: Summary: what to remember (Part 2 of 2)
members.content:
Gases have no fixed shape or volume because their particles move quickly and spread far apart.
Adding or removing heat energy can change matter from one state to another through melting, freezing, evaporating, and condensing.

members.title: Everyday Examples
members.content: An ice cube is a solid, melted ice is liquid water, and water vapor is a gas. These examples show that the same substance can exist in different states. Heating and cooling can cause changes of state, but understanding each state should come first.

materials such as chalk, glass, and dry twigs are rigid and snap instead.

members.title: Hammering delivers a stronger, sharper force. A piece of soft metal that is hammered becomes
members.content: flatter and wider, which is how a panday shapes a bolo or a tansan is flattened into a washer. Brittle materials such as stone and glass do not flatten when hammered; they break into pieces.

347.title: Cutting divides a material into smaller parts, so the change is mainly in size. Paper cut with scissors

members.title: Cutting divides a material into smaller parts, so the change is mainly in size. Paper cut with scissors

347.title: Changes Caused by Heat and by Oxygen (Part 1 of 3)

members.title: Changes Caused by Heat and by Oxygen (Part 1 of 3)
members.content:
The Grade 5 competency moves from force to two conditions that cause deeper changes: application of heat and the presence or lack of oxygen.
Heat can cause a material to melt, evaporate, soften, harden, or burn.
Ice left on a saucer melts into water.

members.title: Changes Caused by Heat and by Oxygen (Part 2 of 3)
members.content:
Candle wax melts and then hardens again when it cools.
Sugar heated in a pan turns brown and gives off a sweet smell as it becomes caramel — and that change cannot be undone.
Oxygen is part of the air around us, and many changes depend on whether it is present.

members.title: Changes Caused by Heat and by Oxygen (Part 3 of 3)
members.content:
Iron exposed to air and moisture forms a reddish-brown coating called rust, which is why a bakal na pako left outdoors during the rainy season looks nothing like a new one.
A candle covered by a glass jar goes out because the oxygen inside is used up.
Sliced saging or mansanas turns brown when left on the table because its exposed flesh reacts with the oxygen in the air.

members.title: Reversible and Irreversible Changes (Part 1 of 3)
members.content:
By Grade 6, learners sort changes into two kinds.
A physical change alters only the appearance of a material — its size, shape, or state — while the material itself stays the same.

members.title: Reversible and Irreversible Changes (Part 2 of 3)
members.content:
Physical changes are usually reversible: melted ice can be frozen again, a crumpled paper can be flattened, and dissolved salt can be recovered by evaporating the water.
A chemical change produces an entirely new material with new properties.

members.title: Reversible and Irreversible Changes (Part 3 of 3)
members.content:
Chemical changes are irreversible: rust cannot be turned back into shiny iron, burnt wood cannot be turned back into wood, and a cooked egg cannot be uncooked.
Useful clues that a chemical change has taken place are a new color, a new smell, bubbles of gas, heat given off, or a solid forming where there was none.

members.title: Useful and Harmful Changes (Part 1 of 3)
members.content:
The last Grade 4 competency asks learners to judge a change, not just describe it.
Many changes are useful.
Cutting cloth produces clothing.
Hammering metal produces tools.
Cooking makes food safe and easier to digest.

members.title: Useful and Harmful Changes (Part 2 of 3)
members.content:
Decaying leaves in a compost pit become fertilizer for a school garden.
Other changes are harmful, especially to the environment.
Rust weakens roofing sheets and bridges.
Spoiled food causes illness.

members.title: Useful and Harmful Changes (Part 3 of 3)
members.content:
Burning plastic and other household waste releases smoke and toxic gases into the air, which is why the practice is discouraged and is covered by the Ecological Solid Waste Management Act.
Learning to tell useful changes from harmful ones is what turns this lesson from a list of observations into a habit of responsible decision-making.
